title: WHO Guideline: Acute Coronary Syndrome and Cardiac Chest Pain
text: Chest pain is a cardinal symptom of acute coronary syndrome (ACS) including STEMI and NSTEMI. Patients over 50 presenting with central crushing chest pain, diaphoresis (sweating), radiation to the jaw, neck, or left arm, and dyspnea (shortness of breath) are at critical risk for acute myocardial infarction. Patients with diabetes or elderly individuals may present with atypical symptoms including silent ischemia, isolated dyspnea, nausea, or fatigue. Immediate 12-lead ECG is mandatory within 10 minutes of presentation. Elevated high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I or T confirms myocardial necrosis. Emergency initial management consists of chewable aspirin (162-325 mg), sublingual nitroglycerin (if systolic BP > 90 mmHg and no right ventricular infarction), supplemental oxygen if SaO2 < 90%, and urgent referral for percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) or thrombolytic therapy if PCI is unavailable.

title: ACC/AHA Guideline: Acute Decompensated Heart Failure
text: Acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF) presents with progressive dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, bilateral lower extremity peripheral edema, and fatigue. Physical examination typically reveals elevated jugular venous distention (JVD), bilateral pulmonary crackles/rales, an S3 gallop, and hepatojugular reflux. Elevated serum B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP > 100 pg/mL) or NT-proBNP (> 300 pg/mL) strongly supports the diagnosis. Chest radiograph demonstrates cardiomegaly, cephalization of pulmonary veins, Kerley B lines, and interstitial edema. Immediate management includes intravenous loop diuretics (e.g. furosemide), vasodilators (nitroglycerin) if hypertensive, and non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (BiPAP/CPAP) for acute respiratory distress. Beta-blockers should not be initiated acutely during severe decompensation.

title: NIH/ACC/AHA Guideline: Hypertension and Hypertensive Emergency
text: Hypertension is defined as sustained systolic blood pressure >= 130 mmHg or diastolic BP >= 80 mmHg. Stage 2 hypertension is BP >= 140/90 mmHg. Hypertensive emergency is defined as acute severe BP elevation (> 180/120 mmHg) with evidence of acute, life-threatening target organ damage (e.g. encephalopathy, acute aortic dissection, pulmonary edema, myocardial infarction, or acute renal failure). Routine outpatient first-line pharmacological treatment includes thiazide diuretics, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), and dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers. In patients with diabetes or chronic kidney disease, ACE inhibitors or ARBs are first-line for nephroprotective benefit. Target BP in diabetic patients is < 130/80 mmHg. In hypertensive emergencies, intravenous agents (labetalol, nicardipine, nitroprusside) are titrated to reduce mean arterial pressure by 20-25% over the first hour.

title: ESC Guideline: Management of Atrial Fibrillation
text: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a supraventricular tachyarrhythmia characterized by uncoordinated atrial activation and irregularly irregular ventricular response. Symptoms include palpitations, lightheadedness, fatigue, exertional dyspnea, and chest discomfort. ECG diagnosis requires absence of distinct P waves, fibrillatory waves, and irregularly irregular RR intervals. Initial management prioritizes hemodynamic stability: synchronized electrical cardioversion is indicated for hemodynamically unstable patients. Rate control is achieved with beta-blockers (metoprolol) or non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (diltiazem, verapamil). Thromboembolic risk is stratified using the CHA2DS2-VASc score (Congestive heart failure, Hypertension, Age >= 75 [2], Diabetes, Stroke [2], Vascular disease, Age 65-74, Sex category). Anticoagulation with DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran) is indicated for males with score >= 2 and females with score >= 3.

title: CDC/IDSA Guideline: Community-Acquired Pneumonia
text: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) presents with acute productive cough, fever (> 38°C), chills, purulent sputum production, dyspnea, and pleuritic chest pain. Physical examination demonstrates localized crackles (rales), bronchial breath sounds, dullness to percussion, and increased tactile fremitus. Chest radiography demonstrating lobar consolidation, patchy alveolar infiltrates, or air bronchograms confirms the diagnosis. Clinical severity is stratified using the CURB-65 criteria (Confusion, Urea > 7 mmol/L, Respiratory rate >= 30/min, low Blood pressure [SBP < 90 or DBP <= 60], Age >= 65). Score 0-1: outpatient treatment; score 2: consider hospital admission; score >= 3: inpatient admission, evaluate for ICU care. First-line outpatient treatment for healthy adults is amoxicillin or doxycycline; for patients with comorbidities (diabetes, COPD, heart disease), combination therapy with amoxicillin/clavulanate plus azithromycin, or respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) is indicated.

title: GOLD/WHO Guideline: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease and Acute Exacerbation
text: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is characterized by persistent, progressive airflow limitation (post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC < 0.70). Major risk factors include cigarette smoking, occupational exposures, and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. Acute exacerbation of COPD (AECOPD) is an acute worsening of respiratory symptoms characterized by the Anthonisen criteria: increased dyspnea, increased sputum volume, and increased sputum purulence. Management of acute exacerbations entails: inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonists (salbutamol) and short-acting anticholinergics (ipratropium), systemic oral corticosteroids (prednisone 40 mg daily for 5 days), and targeted antibiotics (macrolide, doxycycline, or amoxicillin-clavulanate) when sputum purulence is present. Controlled oxygen therapy targeting SpO2 88-92% is essential to avoid hypercapnic respiratory drive suppression.

title: GINA/CDC Guideline: Acute Asthma Exacerbation and Management
text: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways characterized by episodic wheezing, breathlessness, chest tightness, and nighttime or early morning cough. Triggers include viral infections, allergens, cold air, exercise, NSAIDs, and beta-blockers. Acute severe asthma presents with marked tachypnea, tachycardia, inability to complete full sentences in one breath, pulsus paradoxus, and peak expiratory flow (PEF) < 50% of personal best. Life-threatening red flags include a 'silent chest' (exhaustion of airflow), cyanosis, bradycardia, confusion, and normal or elevated PaCO2 on ABG indicating respiratory muscle fatigue. Immediate emergency management includes high-dose inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonist (albuterol) via nebulizer or MDI with spacer, inhaled ipratropium bromide, early systemic corticosteroids (oral prednisolone or IV methylprednisolone), oxygen targeting SpO2 93-95%, and IV magnesium sulfate (2 g IV infusion over 20 min) for severe or refractory broncho-constriction.

title: CHEST/NICE Guideline: Acute Pulmonary Embolism and Deep Vein Thrombosis
text: Pulmonary embolism (PE) occurs when a thromboembolus, typically arising from lower-extremity deep vein thrombosis (DVT), occludes the pulmonary arterial bed. Classic clinical triad includes acute onset pleuritic chest pain, unexplained dyspnea, and tachypnea. Hemoptysis, tachycardia, syncope, and unilateral calf swelling/pain support the diagnosis. Clinical pre-test probability is assessed via Wells Score or Geneva Score. Low-probability patients can be evaluated with high-sensitivity D-dimer testing; a normal D-dimer safely excludes PE. High-probability patients or those with positive D-dimer require CT Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA) or V/Q scan if renal impairment or iodinated contrast allergy exists. Massive PE causes acute hemodynamic instability (systolic BP < 90 mmHg) and requires emergency systemic thrombolysis (e.g. alteplase) or surgical embolectomy. Hemodynamically stable PE is managed with immediate therapeutic anticoagulation using DOACs (rivaroxaban, apixaban) or low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH).

title: AHA/ASA/WHO Guideline: Acute Ischemic Stroke Evaluation and Thrombolysis
text: Acute ischemic stroke represents sudden vascular compromise causing focal neurological deficits. Common presentations include unilateral hemiparesis or facial droop, acute slurred speech or aphasia, ataxia, visual field loss, and hemisensory deficits. Pre-hospital identification uses the FAST algorithm (Face droop, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call emergency). Emergency non-contrast head CT is critical immediately on arrival to rule out intracranial hemorrhage prior to reperfusion therapy. Intravenous thrombolysis with recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (alteplase 0.9 mg/kg or tenecteplase) is indicated within 4.5 hours of symptom onset provided BP < 185/110 mmHg and no contraindications (recent major surgery, active bleeding, severe thrombocytopenia). Endovascular mechanical thrombectomy is indicated for large vessel occlusion (LVO) in the anterior circulation within 6-24 hours of last known normal.

title: NICE Guideline: Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA) and Secondary Prevention
text: A Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA) is defined as a transient episode of neurological dysfunction caused by focal brain, spinal cord, or retinal ischemia, without acute infarction on neuroimaging. Symptoms typically resolve completely within 1 hour. Short-term risk of full stroke following TIA is high, especially within the first 48 hours. Risk stratification uses the ABCD2 score (Age >= 60, Blood pressure >= 140/90, Clinical features [unilateral weakness=2, speech disturbance=1], Duration [>=60 min=2, 10-59 min=1], and Diabetes). Immediate specialist neurological assessment within 24 hours is required. Immediate antiplatelet therapy consists of aspirin 300 mg daily, followed by dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + clopidogrel) for 21 days for high-risk TIA. Carotid Doppler ultrasound should be performed urgently to identify severe carotid stenosis amenable to carotid endarterectomy.

title: IDSA/AES Guideline: Acute Bacterial Meningitis and Status Epilepticus
text: Acute bacterial meningitis is an emergency characterized by the classic triad of fever, altered mental status, and nuchal rigidity (neck stiffness). Positive Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs indicate meningeal irritation. Headache, photophobia, and petechial or purpuric rash (characteristic of Neisseria meningitidis) may be present. Immediate blood cultures followed by empirical IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone + vancomycin + ampicillin if > 50yo for Listeria coverage) and adjunctive IV dexamethasone must be administered without delay. Lumbar puncture should not delay antibiotic administration. Status epilepticus is defined as continuous seizure activity >= 5 minutes or recurrent seizures without return to baseline. First-line treatment is IV lorazepam (4 mg) or IM midazolam (10 mg), followed immediately by second-line IV antiseizure medications: levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, or valproate sodium.

title: NICE/ADA Guideline: Type 2 Diabetes Management and Hyperglycemic Crises
text: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is characterized by progressive insulin secretory defect on the background of insulin resistance. Diagnostic criteria: fasting plasma glucose >= 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L), HbA1c >= 6.5% (48 mmol/mol), or 2-hour post-OGTT glucose >= 200 mg/dL. Classic presentation includes polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, fatigue, and blurred vision. First-line pharmacotherapy is metformin, with dose titration up to 2000 mg/day (monitor eGFR; avoid if eGFR < 30 mL/min). For patients with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure, or chronic kidney disease, SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) or GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide) with demonstrated cardiovascular and renal benefit are added regardless of baseline HbA1c. Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and Hyperglycemic Hyperosmolar State (HHS) are medical emergencies requiring vigorous IV 0.9% saline fluid resuscitation, regular insulin infusion (0.1 units/kg/h), and potassium monitoring and repletion before insulin administration if K+ < 3.3 mEq/L.

title: ATA/NICE Guideline: Hypothyroidism and Thyroid Disorders
text: Primary hypothyroidism is characterized by insufficient thyroid hormone production from the thyroid gland, most commonly due to Hashimoto's autoimmune thyroiditis. Symptoms include chronic fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, dry coarse skin, periorbital puffiness, non-pitting myxedema, and delayed relaxation phase of deep tendon reflexes. Laboratory diagnosis demonstrates elevated serum Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH) with decreased free thyroxine (free T4). Subclinical hypothyroidism displays elevated TSH with normal free T4. First-line replacement therapy is oral levothyroxine (T4) administered once daily on an empty stomach 30-60 minutes before breakfast. Standard full replacement dose is approximately 1.6 mcg/kg/day in young healthy adults. In elderly patients or those with coronary artery disease, start with a lower dose (25-50 mcg daily) to prevent precipitation of angina or arrhythmias. Monitor serum TSH every 6 to 8 weeks after dose adjustment until euthyroid.

title: NICE Guideline: Uncomplicated Lower Urinary Tract Infection (Cystitis)
text: Uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection (cystitis) occurs primarily in non-pregnant adult females with a structurally normal urinary tract. Classic triad of lower tract symptoms: dysuria (burning sensation on micturition), urinary frequency, and urinary urgency. Suprapubic discomfort and micro/macro-hematuria may accompany cystitis. Absence of fever, chills, rigors, nausea/vomiting, and costovertebral angle (CVA) flank tenderness differentiates uncomplicated cystitis from acute pyelonephritis. Urine dipstick testing showing positive leukocyte esterase and nitrites supports bacterial infection (most commonly Escherichia coli). First-line empirical antimicrobial therapy: nitrofurantoin 100 mg orally twice daily for 5 days, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) 160/800 mg twice daily for 3 days (if local E. coli resistance < 20%), or fosfomycin trometamol 3 g single oral dose. Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin) are reserved for complicated infections due to adverse effect profiles.

title: IDSA/NICE Guideline: Acute Pyelonephritis and Upper UTI
text: Acute pyelonephritis is an invasive bacterial infection of the renal parenchyma and collecting system. Clinical presentation includes fever (> 38°C), shaking chills, unilateral or bilateral costovertebral angle (CVA) tenderness (flank pain), nausea, vomiting, and systemic malaise, frequently accompanied by lower urinary tract symptoms (dysuria, frequency). Urinalysis reveals pyuria, bacteriuria, and white blood cell (WBC) casts, which are pathognomonic for upper tract renal involvement. Blood and urine cultures should be obtained in all patients prior to initiating antibiotic therapy. Mild-to-moderate outpatient pyelonephritis can be treated with oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 7 days or levofloxacin 750 mg daily for 5 days. Hospitalization and IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone, piperacillin-tazobactam) are required for pregnant women, severe dehydration, inability to tolerate oral medications, hemodynamic instability, or suspicion of urinary tract obstruction/calculus.

title: KDIGO Guideline: Acute Kidney Injury Evaluation and Staging
text: Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) is defined by KDIGO criteria as any of: increase in serum creatinine by >= 0.3 mg/dL (26.5 umol/L) within 48 hours; or increase in serum creatinine to >= 1.5 times baseline within 7 days; or urine output < 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours. Etiologies are categorized into: 1. Pre-renal: intravascular volume depletion, sepsis, heart failure, NSAID/ACEi hemodynamic effects (BUN/Cr ratio > 20:1, FeNa < 1%). 2. Intrinsic renal: acute tubular necrosis (ATN, muddy brown granular casts), acute interstitial nephritis (AIN, drug-induced, eosinophils), glomerulonephritis (RBC casts, proteinuria). 3. Post-renal: bilateral urinary tract obstruction, benign prostatic hyperplasia, obstructing calculi (hydronephrosis on renal ultrasound). Immediate management involves discontinuing all nephrotoxic medications (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, IV contrast), correcting volume status, and treating hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, and volume overload.

title: WAO/NICE Guideline: Anaphylaxis Emergency Recognition and Treatment
text: Anaphylaxis is an acute, life-threatening systemic hypersensitivity reaction characterized by rapid onset of airway, breathing, or circulatory compromise. Diagnostic criteria: sudden onset of mucosal/skin symptoms (generalized hives/urticaria, pruritus, flushing, swollen lips/tongue/uvula/angioedema) PLUS at least one of: 1. Respiratory compromise: dyspnea, wheezing, stridor, hypoxemia. 2. Reduced blood pressure or end-organ dysfunction: hypotension (SBP < 90 mmHg or > 30% decrease from baseline), syncope, incontinence, diaphoresis. Common triggers include foods (peanuts, tree nuts, shellfish), medications (beta-lactam antibiotics, NSAIDs), and insect venoms. FIRST-LINE TREATMENT IS IMMEDIATE INTRAMUSCULAR (IM) EPINEPHRINE (adrenaline) 0.01 mg/kg, maximum 0.5 mg in adults (0.3 mg in children), injected into the anterolateral mid-thigh. Do not delay epinephrine for antihistamines or corticosteroids! Repeat epinephrine every 5-15 minutes if symptoms persist. Place patient in recumbent position with elevated legs. Secondary adjunctive treatments include IV crystalloid fluid boluses (1-2 L 0.9% saline) for hypotension, nebulized albuterol for bronchospasm, and H1/H2 antihistamines and IV corticosteroids to prevent protracted or biphasic reactions.

title: Surviving Sepsis Campaign: Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock
text: Sepsis is defined as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection (SOFA score increase >= 2 points). Quick SOFA (qSOFA) bedside screening uses 3 criteria: respiratory rate >= 22/min, altered mentation (GCS < 15), and systolic BP <= 100 mmHg. Septic shock is defined as sepsis requiring vasopressors to maintain MAP >= 65 mmHg and serum lactate > 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation. The Sepsis Hour-1 Bundle requires immediate implementation: 1. Measure serum lactate level; remeasure if initial lactate > 2 mmol/L. 2. Obtain blood cultures prior to administration of antibiotics. 3. Administer broad-spectrum empiric IV antimicrobials within 1 hour. 4. Rapidly infuse 30 mL/kg crystalloid fluid for hypotension (MAP < 65 mmHg) or lactate >= 4 mmol/L. 5. Apply vasopressors (norepinephrine is first-line) during or after fluid resuscitation to maintain MAP >= 65 mmHg.

title: ACG Guideline: Gastritis, Peptic Ulcer Disease, and H. Pylori
text: Gastritis and Peptic Ulcer Disease (PUD) present with burning epigastric pain, dyspepsia, early satiety, postprandial fullness, and nausea. Duodenal ulcer pain typically improves with meals and recurs 2-3 hours later or at night, whereas gastric ulcer pain is frequently exacerbated by food ingestion. Major etiologies include Helicobacter pylori infection and extensive nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) or aspirin use. Alarm 'red flag' features requiring urgent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy (EGD) include: gastrointestinal bleeding (melena, hematemesis), unintentional weight loss, progressive dysphagia or odynophagia, persistent vomiting, palpable abdominal mass, or new onset in patients > 55 years of age. Diagnostic testing for H. pylori includes urea breath test, stool antigen assay, or endoscopic biopsy. First-line treatment is proton pump inhibitor (PPI) therapy (omeprazole 20-40 mg daily) and H. pylori eradication therapy (bismuth quadruple therapy: PPI + bismuth subsalicylate + metronidazole + tetracycline for 14 days).

title: WSES/ACG Guideline: Acute Appendicitis and Acute Pancreatitis
text: Acute appendicitis begins with periumbilical visceral pain that migrates to the right lower quadrant (McBurney's point) within 12-24 hours. Physical exam reveals localized tenderness, involuntary guarding, rebound tenderness, Rovsing's sign, psoas sign, and obturator sign. Leukocytosis with left shift and elevated CRP are common. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT confirms diagnosis (appendix diameter > 6 mm). Definitive treatment is urgent laparoscopic appendectomy and IV perioperative antibiotics. Acute pancreatitis presents with severe, constant, boring epigastric pain that radiates directly to the back, exacerbated by lying supine and relieved by leaning forward. Diagnosis requires 2 of 3 criteria: characteristic abdominal pain; serum lipase or amylase > 3 times the upper limit of normal; characteristic findings on contrast-enhanced CT or MRI. Etiologies: gallstones (40%), alcohol (35%), hypertriglyceridemia, hypercalcemia. Management: aggressive IV fluid resuscitation (lactated Ringer's), early enteral nutrition, and analgesia.

title: NIH/WHO Guideline: COVID-19 Clinical Presentation and Antiviral Therapy
text: Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19), caused by SARS-CoV-2, presents with fever, dry cough, profound fatigue, dyspnea, sore throat, congestion, headache, myalgia, and sudden loss of taste (ageusia) or smell (anosmia). Gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea, diarrhea) occur in 10-20% of patients. Severe illness features hypoxemic respiratory failure (SpO2 < 94% on room air), ARDS, thromboembolism, and hyperinflammatory cytokine release. In outpatients with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 at high risk of progression to severe disease (age >= 65, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, obesity, immunosuppression), first-line treatment is oral nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (Paxlovid) initiated within 5 days of symptom onset. Hospitalized patients requiring supplemental oxygen receive dexamethasone (6 mg daily for up to 10 days) and remdesivir; baricitinib or tocilizumab is added for rapidly deteriorating patients with systemic inflammation.

title: CDC Guideline: Seasonal Influenza Presentation and Antiviral Treatment
text: Seasonal Influenza (Flu) presents abruptly with high fever (38-40°C), severe myalgia, arthralgia, headache, prostration, non-productive dry cough, sore throat, and rhinitis. In contrast to the common cold, onset is sudden and systemic constitutional symptoms predominate. Complications include primary viral pneumonia, secondary bacterial pneumonia (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus), myositis, myocarditis, and exacerbation of underlying chronic pulmonary or cardiac conditions. Antiviral treatment with neuraminidase inhibitors (oral oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days) is recommended as early as possible for any patient with confirmed or suspected influenza who is hospitalized, has severe/complicated illness, or is at high risk for influenza complications (adults >= 65, young children, pregnant women, immunocompromised, chronic medical conditions). Greatest clinical benefit is achieved when started within 48 hours of symptom onset.

title: IDSA Guideline: Streptococcal Pharyngitis and Skin/Soft Tissue Infections
text: Group A Streptococcal (GAS) pharyngitis presents with sudden-onset sore throat, pain on swallowing (odynophagia), fever, tonsillopharyngeal erythema with tonsillar exudates, and tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy. Absence of viral symptoms (cough, rhinorrhea, conjunctivitis, hoarseness) strongly favors GAS (Centor criteria). First-line treatment is oral penicillin V or oral amoxicillin for 10 days to prevent acute rheumatic fever and peritonsillar abscess. Cellulitis is an acute, spreading bacterial infection of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue characterized by localized erythema, warmth, edema, and tenderness, most commonly caused by Streptococcus pyogenes or Staphylococcus aureus. Purulent cellulitis (abscess, furuncle) mandates incision and drainage with coverage for community-acquired MRSA (TMP-SMX, doxycycline, or vancomycin).

title: ACR Guideline: Acute Gouty Arthritis and Hyperuricemia
text: Gout is an inflammatory arthritis triggered by monosodium urate crystal deposition in articular and periarticular tissues. Acute gout attack presents with sudden, excruciating pain, erythema, warmth, and marked swelling, classically affecting the first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint (podagra) or ankles/knees. Symptoms frequently begin abruptly overnight. Definitive diagnosis requires arthrocentesis demonstrating needle-shaped, negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals under polarized light microscopy. Acute flare pharmacotherapy: low-dose oral colchicine (1.2 mg at flare onset followed by 0.6 mg 1 hour later), oral NSAIDs (indomethacin, naproxen), or systemic corticosteroids (prednisone 30-40 mg daily) if NSAIDs/colchicine are contraindicated (renal failure, heart failure). Urate-lowering therapy with allopurinol (xanthine oxidase inhibitor) is indicated for recurrent flares, tophi, or radiographic joint damage.

title: ASH Guideline: Iron Deficiency Anemia and Microcytic Anemias
text: Iron Deficiency Anemia (IDA) is the most common cause of anemia worldwide. Symptoms include chronic fatigue, generalized weakness, exertional dyspnea, dizziness, pallor, cold extremities, pica (craving ice/dirt), and brittle nails with spooning (koilonychia). Complete blood count demonstrates microcytic, hypochromic anemia (hemoglobin < 13 g/dL in men, < 12 g/dL in women; mean corpuscular volume MCV < 80 fL). Diagnostic iron studies confirm low serum ferritin (< 30 ng/mL, the most specific test), low serum iron, elevated total iron-binding capacity (TIBC), and transferrin saturation < 16%. In men and postmenopausal women, IDA mandates full gastrointestinal endoscopic evaluation (colonoscopy and EGD) to rule out occult gastrointestinal malignancy. Treatment involves oral ferrous sulfate (or modern alternate-day dosing) with ascorbic acid, or intravenous iron for intolerance or malabsorption.

title: APA/NICE Guideline: Panic Attacks and Panic Disorder
text: A panic attack is a discrete, intense surge of fear or discomfort that reaches a peak within minutes, accompanied by at least 4 somatic/cognitive symptoms: palpitations or tachycardia, sweating, trembling/shaking, shortness of breath or smothering sensations, choking feeling, chest pain or discomfort, nausea or abdominal distress, dizziness/unsteadiness, derealization or depersonalization, fear of losing control, and fear of impending death. Crucially, life-threatening somatic emergencies (acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary embolism, arrhythmia, pheochromocytoma, thyroid storm) must be ruled out before attributing chest pain and dyspnea solely to a panic attack. First-line maintenance treatment for panic disorder includes selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs: sertraline, escitalopram) and cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT). Short-acting benzodiazepines may be used for immediate acute termination but carry dependence risks.

title: AAD Guideline: Atopic Dermatitis, Shingles (Herpes Zoster), and Acute Rashes
text: Atopic dermatitis (eczema) is a chronic pruritic inflammatory skin disorder characterized by intensely itchy erythematous papules, excoriations, and lichenification, typically involving flexural surfaces (antecubital and popliteal fossae). Management centers on emollient barrier repair and topical corticosteroids for acute flares. Herpes Zoster (Shingles) results from reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus (VZV) in sensory dorsal root ganglia. It presents with a prodrome of dermatomal pain, burning, or tingling followed by a unilateral, painful eruption of grouped vesicles on an erythematous base strictly limited to a single dermatome. Oral antiviral therapy with valacyclovir (1000 mg 3 times daily) or acyclovir initiated within 72 hours of rash onset accelerates lesion healing and reduces the incidence of postherpetic neuralgia. Involvement of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve (Hutchinson's sign on nose tip) mandates urgent ophthalmology consult.

title: AAP Guideline: Pediatric Croup, Bronchiolitis, and Febrile Illness
text: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) is a viral respiratory illness in young children (6 months to 3 years) typically caused by parainfluenza virus. It presents with a distinctive 'seal-bark' cough, inspiratory stridor, hoarseness, and low-grade fever, often worsening at night. Single-dose oral dexamethasone (0.15-0.6 mg/kg) is standard first-line therapy for all severities; nebulized racemic epinephrine is added for moderate-to-severe stridor at rest. Bronchiolitis, commonly caused by Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) in infants < 12 months, presents with rhinorrhea, tachypnea, wheezing, subcostal retractions, and poor feeding. Treatment is supportive: nasal suctioning, gentle hydration, and supplemental oxygen if SpO2 < 90%. Bronchodilators and systemic steroids are not routinely recommended in viral bronchiolitis.

title: WHO Guideline: Management of Cardiac Chest Pain
text: Chest pain is a cardinal symptom of acute coronary syndrome (ACS). Patients over 60 with chest pain, diaphoresis, and a history of diabetes or hypertension are at high risk for myocardial infarction. Immediate 12-lead ECG is recommended within 10 minutes of presentation. Elevated cardiac troponin confirms myocardial injury. Management includes aspirin 162-325 mg chewed, nitroglycerin if blood pressure permits, and urgent percutaneous coronary intervention for STEMI. Cardiac biomarkers should be measured at baseline and 3-6 hours later. Diabetic patients may present with atypical chest pain or silent ischemia.

title: CDC Guideline: Community-Acquired Pneumonia
text: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) presents with cough, fever, sputum production, dyspnea, and pleuritic chest pain. Physical exam may reveal crackles, bronchial breath sounds, and tactile fremitus. Chest X-ray showing lobar consolidation confirms diagnosis. The CURB-65 score (Confusion, Urea, Respiratory rate, Blood pressure, Age >= 65) stratifies severity. First-line outpatient treatment for healthy adults is amoxicillin or a macrolide. Hospitalized patients receive ceftriaxone plus azithromycin. Elderly patients (>65) with comorbidities such as diabetes have worse outcomes and warrant hospital admission. Vaccination with pneumococcal conjugate vaccine is recommended for adults 65 and older.

title: NICE Guideline: Type 2 Diabetes Management
text: Type 2 diabetes mellitus is characterized by insulin resistance and relative insulin deficiency. Diagnostic criteria include fasting plasma glucose >= 126 mg/dL, HbA1c >= 6.5%, or random glucose >= 200 mg/dL with symptoms. First-line pharmacotherapy is metformin for most patients. SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 receptor agonists are preferred when cardiovascular disease or high risk exists. Blood pressure target is < 130/80 mmHg. Statins are recommended for patients 40-75 with diabetes. Annual screening for retinopathy, nephropathy, and neuropathy is mandatory. Metformin should be dose-adjusted in renal impairment (eGFR < 45).

title: NIH Guideline: Hypertension Management
text: Hypertension is defined as sustained blood pressure >= 130/80 mmHg per current ACC/AHA guidelines. Stage 2 hypertension is >= 140/90 mmHg. First-line antihypertensives include thiazide diuretics, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, and calcium channel blockers. For patients with diabetes and hypertension, ACE inhibitors or ARBs are preferred due to renal protective effects. Target blood pressure in diabetics is < 130/80 mmHg. Combination therapy is often required for achieving target. Lifestyle modifications: DASH diet, sodium restriction < 1500 mg/day, aerobic exercise 150 min/week, weight loss, alcohol moderation.

title: WHO Guideline: COPD Management
text: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is characterized by persistent respiratory symptoms and airflow limitation due to airway/alveolar abnormalities. Diagnosis requires spirometry showing FEV1/FVC < 0.70 post-bronchodilator. Symptoms include chronic cough, sputum, and progressive dyspnea. Smoking is the leading risk factor. GOLD classification stages A-D guide therapy. Initial therapy for Group D includes LAMA/LABA combination. Inhaled corticosteroids are added for exacerbations. Acute exacerbations present with increased dyspnea, sputum volume, or purulence. Treatment of exacerbations: short-acting bronchodilators, systemic corticosteroids (prednisone 40 mg for 5 days), and antibiotics if increased sputum purulence.

title: CDC Guideline: Asthma Management
text: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disease with reversible airflow obstruction. Diagnosis rests on history of wheeze, dyspnea, chest tightness, and cough, plus reversible airflow limitation on spirometry (FEV1 improvement >= 12% and 200 mL post-bronchodilator). Stepwise treatment: Step 1 short-acting beta-agonist (SABA) PRN. Step 2 adds low-dose inhaled corticosteroid (ICS). Step 3 ICS plus LABA. Step 4 medium-dose ICS plus LABA. Step 5-high-dose ICS/LABA with or without biologic (omalizumab, mepolizumab). Asthma exacerbations: oxygen, SABA via nebulization, systemic corticosteroids, and consider magnesium sulfate in severe cases. Avoid triggers and ensure inhaler technique adherence.

title: NICE Guideline: Urinary Tract Infection
text: Uncomplicated urinary tract infection (UTI) typically presents with dysuria, frequency, urgency, and suprapubic discomfort. Complicated UTI features fever, flank pain, or signs of pyelonephritis. Diagnosis is confirmed by positive urinalysis (nitrites, leukocyte esterase) and urine culture with >= 10^3 CFU/mL. First-line treatment for uncomplicated cystitis in non-pregnant women: nitrofurantoin 100 mg BD for 5 days, or trimethoprim 200 mg BD for 3 days. Pregnant women require 7-day course, avoiding trimethoprim in first trimester. Pyelonephritis: ceftriaxone IV or oral fluoroquinolone. Recurrent UTIs warrant investigation for structural or functional abnormalities.

title: WHO Guideline: Sepsis Management
text: Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by dysregulated host response to infection. The SOFA score (Sequential Organ Failure Assessment) identifies organ dysfunction. Septic shock is sepsis with fluids unresponsive hypotension requiring vasopressors and elevated lactate > 2 mmol/L. Management follows Hour-1 bundle: measure lactate, obtain blood cultures, administer broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, begin crystalloid 30 mL/kg, and apply vasopressors if hypotensive. The qSOFA screen (altered mentation, RR >= 22, SBP <= 100) identifies high-risk patients. Lactate clearance and ongoing organ support in ICU reduce mortality. Early recognition is critical.

title: COVID-19: Diagnosis and Management Review
text: COVID-19, caused by SARS-CoV-2, presents with fever, cough, dyspnea, fatigue, myalgia, and loss of taste/smell. Severe disease features hypoxia and bilateral infiltrates on chest imaging. Diagnosis confirmed by RT-PCR or rapid antigen testing. Risk factors for severe disease: age > 65, diabetes, hypertension, obesity, immunocompromised state. Mild disease is managed symptomatically. Moderate-severe disease requires antiviral therapy (nirmatrelvir-ritonavir in outpatients within 5 days), dexamethasone 6 mg for those requiring oxygen, and prophylactic anticoagulation. Long COVID characterized by persistent symptoms > 12 weeks warrants follow-up.

title: NICE Guideline: Hypothyroidism
text: Primary hypothyroidism is defined by elevated TSH and low free T4. Symptoms are insidious: fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, bradycardia, and cognitive slowing. Most common cause in iodine-sufficient areas is Hashimoto's autoimmune thyroiditis, characterized by positive anti-TPO antibodies. Treatment is levothyroxine, dosed by weight (1.6 mcg/kg/day). Starting dose in younger healthy adults is full replacement; in elderly or cardiac disease, start low (25 mcg) and titrate every 4-6 weeks based on TSH. Target TSH is 0.4-4.0 mIU/L. Subclinical hypothyroidism (elevated TSH, normal T4) warrants treatment if TSH > 10 or symptomatic.

title: WHO Guideline: Acute Stroke Management
text: Acute stroke is sudden neurological deficit from cerebral ischemia or hemorrhage. The FAST acronym (Face, Arm, Speech, Time) aids recognition. Non-contrast CT head distinguishes ischemic from hemorrhagic stroke. Ischemic stroke treated with IV thrombolysis (alteplase) within 4.5 hours of symptom onset if no contraindications; mechanical thrombectomy for large vessel occlusion within 6-24 hours. Blood pressure management: permissive hypertension (<= 220/120) for ischemic stroke; target SBP < 140 for hemorrhagic stroke. Secondary prevention includes antiplatelet therapy (aspirin 81 mg), statin, blood pressure control, and glycemic management in diabetics.

title: Primer on Acute Kidney Injury
text: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is abrupt decrease in renal function. KDIGO criteria: rise in creatinine >= 0.3 mg/dL within 48h, or >= 1.5x baseline, or urine output < 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours. Causes are pre-renal (hypovolemia, heart failure), intrinsic (acute tubular necrosis, glomerulonephritis), or post-renal (obstruction). Management: identify and treat underlying cause, restore intravascular volume, avoid nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, contrast). Indications for dialysis (AEIOU): Acidosis, Electrolyte disturbances, Ingestion, Overload, Uremia. Patients with diabetic nephropathy are at higher risk of contrast-induced AKI;pre-hydration and low-contrast protocols are recommended.

title: CDC Guideline: Seasonal Influenza
text: Influenza is an acute viral respiratory illness caused by influenza A and B. Symptoms include abrupt onset fever, chills, myalgia, headache, sore throat, and cough. Diagnosis via rapid antigen testing or RT-PCR. Antiviral treatment (oseltamivir 75 mg BD for 5 days) started within 48 hours of symptom onset reduces severity and duration. Hospitalization is required for dyspnea, hypoxia, or dehydration. High-risk groups (age > 65, pregnancy, chronic lung/heart disease, diabetes) warrant empiric antiviral treatment regardless of symptom duration. Annual influenza vaccination is the most effective prevention. Elderly patients may have atypical presentations without fever.

title: NICE Guideline: Anaphylaxis
text: Anaphylaxis is a severe systemic allergic reaction with rapid onset and airway/breathing/circulation compromise. Common triggers: foods (peanuts, shellfish), medications (penicillin, NSAIDs), insect stings. Clinical features: urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, hypotension, hypoxia. Immediate treatment is intramuscular epinephrine 0.5 mg (adult), repeated every 5 minutes if unresponsive. Adjuncts: oxygen, IV fluids, H1/H2 antihistamines, corticosteroids. Patients on beta-blockers may be refractory to epinephrine; consider glucagon. Disposition: observation 6-12 hours for biphasic reaction risk. Confirm known allergies in patient history and avoid triggers.

title: Review: Acute Gastritis and Peptic Ulcer Disease
text: Acute gastritis presents with epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. Common causes: NSAID use, alcohol, Helicobacter pylori infection, and stress. Peptic ulcer disease (PUD) features epigastric pain relieved by food or antacids in duodenal ulcers, or worsened by food in gastric ulcers. Diagnosis: esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD), H. pylori testing (urea breath test, stool antigen). Treatment: proton pump inhibitor (omeprazole 20-40 mg) for 4-8 weeks. H. pylori eradication: triple therapy (PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin) for 14 days. Stop NSAIDs; consider misoprostol for NSAID users. Seek urgent care if hematemesis, melena, or severe pain (possible perforation).

title: CDC: Cardiac Biomarkers in Acute Coronary Syndrome
text: In patients presenting with chest pain suspicious for acute coronary syndrome, high-sensitivity cardiac troponin is the biomarker of choice. Obtain a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes. Serial troponin measurements at 0 and 3 hours (or 1-2 hours with high-sensitivity assays) enable rapid rule-out or rule-in of myocardial infarction. A rise and/or fall in troponin with at least one value above the 99th percentile upper reference limit indicates myocardial injury. Ischemia is suggested by symptoms or ECG changes. Coronary angiography is indicated for non-ST elevation ACS with high-risk features such as dynamic ECG changes, elevated troponin, or hemodynamic instability. Patients with diabetes often have silent or atypical ischemia.

title: WHO: Hospital Management of Severe Pneumonia
text: Severe community-acquired pneumonia requires hospital admission and empiric antibiotics. Empiric coverage for hospitalized patients includes a beta-lactam plus a macrolide (e.g., ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily). For patients with risk factors for resistant organisms, broader coverage is needed. Supportive care includes oxygen for hypoxia, intravenous fluids, and antipyretics. Assess CURB-65: confusion, urea > 7 mmol/L, respiratory rate >= 30, blood pressure low, and age >= 65. A score of 3 or more suggests severe disease and ICU admission should be considered. Monitor for treatment failure if fever persists beyond 72 hours.

title: Recurrent and Complicated Urinary Tract Infections
text: Urinary tract infection is diagnosed by symptoms of dysuria, frequency, urgency, and a positive urine culture. Uncomplicated cystitis in young women is usually caused by Escherichia coli. First-line short-course therapy includes nitrofurantoin or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Pyelonephritis, indicated by fever and flank pain, requires 7-14 days of treatment and typically a fluoroquinolone or ceftriaxone. Complicated UTI risk factors include pregnancy, diabetes, immunosuppression, and urinary obstruction. In men, UTI suggests possible prostatitis and warrants longer therapy. Recurrent cystitis in women can be managed with post-coital prophylaxis or continuous low-dose antibiotics. Hydration and voiding after intercourse reduce recurrence risk.

title: Management of COPD Exacerbations
text: An acute exacerbation of COPD is an acute worsening of respiratory symptoms that requires additional therapy. Cardinal symptoms are increased dyspnea, increased sputum volume, and increased sputum purulence. Treatment includes short-acting bronchodilators (inhaled beta-agonists and anticholinergics), systemic corticosteroids such as prednisone 40 mg daily for five days, and antibiotics when sputum is purulent. Oxygen therapy titrated to 88-92% saturation prevents hypercapnia. Noninvasive ventilation (NIV) reduces intubation in acute hypercapnic respiratory failure. Hospitalization is warranted for severe dyspnea, altered mental status, or hypoxia. Smoking cessation and vaccination reduce future exacerbations.

title: NICE: Anaphylaxis Emergency Treatment
text: Anaphylaxis is an acute, life-threatening systemic reaction. First-line treatment is intramuscular epinephrine 0.5 mg in adults and 0.01 mg/kg in children, repeated every 5 minutes if no improvement. Place the patient supine with legs elevated unless airway compromise. Administer high-flow oxygen and rapid IV fluid bolus for hypotension. Antihistamines (H1 and H2) and corticosteroids are adjunctive, not life-saving. Beta-blocked patients may be epinephrine-resistant; consider glucagon. Observe all patients for at least 6 hours due to risk of biphasic reactions. Discharge with an epinephrine auto-injector and an allergist referral.

title: Update: Levothyroxine Dosing in Hypothyroidism
text: Primary hypothyroidism is confirmed by a persistently elevated TSH with a low free thyroxine (T4). Typical symptoms include fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, and cognitive slowing. Treatment is levothyroxine, approximately 1.6 mcg/kg/day. In healthy adults under 60, start at the full estimated replacement dose. In patients over 60 or with cardiac disease, start at 25-50 mcg and titrate slowly to avoid precipitating arrhythmia. Recheck TSH in 6-8 weeks and adjust by 12.5-25 mcg increments. In pregnancy, levothyroxine requirements increase by about 30%. Subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH 4-10 with normal T4) is treated when TSH is above 10 or when symptoms or pregnancy are present.

title: WHO: IV Thrombolysis for Acute Ischemic Stroke
text: Acute ischemic stroke is treated with intravenous alteplase within 4.5 hours of last-known-well, provided no contraindications. Rapid recognition via the FAST screen (face, arm, speech, time) and immediate brain imaging are essential. Mechanical thrombectomy is offered for large vessel occlusion up to 24 hours. Blood pressure is managed to less than 185/110 mmHg before thrombolysis. Exclude hemorrhagic stroke with non-contrast CT before treatment. Antiplatelets should be avoided for 24 hours after alteplase. Early dysphagia screening reduces aspiration pneumonia. Secondary prevention includes antiplatelets, statins, blood pressure control, and anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation.

title: NICE: Pyelonephritis Management
text: Pyelonephritis is an infection of the renal pelvis and kidney, typically presenting with fever, chills, flank pain, nausea, and dysuria. Urinalysis shows pyuria and often nitrites. A urine culture confirms the organism; blood cultures are reserved for severe disease. Outpatient treatment for uncomplicated pyelonephritis is oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily or levofloxacin 750 mg daily for 7 days. Pregnant patients and those who are septic require hospitalization with IV ceftriaxone. Assess for complicating factors such as obstruction or stones when fever persists beyond 72 hours. Analgesia and hydration are supportive. Diabetes increases risk of complicated infection and bacteremia.

title: NICE Guideline: Assessment and Management of Headaches in Over 12s
text: Headaches are classified into primary (tension-type headache, migraine, cluster headache) and secondary headaches. Tension-type headache presents with bilateral, pressing or tightening band-like headache of mild to moderate intensity, without nausea or vomiting. Migraine presents with recurrent moderate to severe headache episodes, typically unilateral and throbbing or pulsating, aggravated by routine physical activity, and accompanied by nausea, photophobia, or phonophobia. Triptans, NSAIDs, and paracetamol are first-line acute treatments. Red flags warranting urgent escalation include sudden onset thunderclap headache, systemic symptoms with fever, and new focal neurological deficits.
